newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam's Muoi says shield farmers from exploiters.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam's Muoi says shield farmers from exploiters.

text.p: Vietnam's top official, 80-year-old Do Muoi, has called for measures to protect farmers and warned that a system where they had no choice but to sell crops at low prices to private traders would not be tolerated.

The veteran communist party chief was quoted in state media on Thursday as telling members of the Vietnam Farmers' Association they should establish new socialist cooperatives to improve the sale and processing of commodities.
"He said that a situation where farmers were unhappy although they had produced bumper crops of rice and vegetables would not be tolerated," Vietnam News quoted him as saying.
"He said rice was stockpiled and farmers were at the mercy of the low prices offered by private traders."
Muoi added that the Farmers' Association needed to educate individual farmers about the ineffectiveness of working separately.
Around 80 percent of Vietnam's 77 million population derive a living from farming and commodities including rice and coffee are major export earners.

This year's winter-spring rice crop in the Mekong Delta and good yields in the northern Red River Delta have resulted in bumper harvests. According to U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) estimates, Vietnam's 1996/97 rice crop will have produced 27.4 million tonnes.
But a recent USDA report said Vietnam was also likely to sell less rice abroad than it had hoped for because of export disputes and weakening global demand.
Traders say capricious behaviour by state-owned exporters has caused buyers to turn to Thailand for rice, despite higher prices there.
Another problem is a state-controlled pricing system that sees middle-men and state exporters offering less than market prices to farmers for their unmilled rice.

Muoi's comments closely echoed those of senior adviser Nguyen Van Linh who warned recently that social ills were growing among rural communities where exploitation by wealthy landowners and private traders was causing individual farmers to suffer.

"In many localities, state-run enterprises, for some reason, did not purchase or bought only a very small volume of rice from the peasants," he said. "In such conditions, private traders can bargain for lower prices from the peasants and the latter have no choice but to sell..."
